strengths: Mathematically sound use of topological covering maps to lift interval-valued quantities to cyclic groups, elegantly addressing the limitation of prior work (LCER)
Dramatic quantitative improvements in equivariance error: 4.66×10⁻⁶ for T³CEN vs 0.445 for LCER, with lifting error six orders of magnitude lower

Comprehensive experimental validation across synthetic datasets (3D Shapes, Small NORB), natural images (CIFAR, Caltech), and medical imaging (Camelyon17) with proper use of random seeds and error bars
Principled entropy-based approach to group order selection (Section 5.4, Figure 6) rather than arbitrary hyperparameter choices
Generalizability beyond HSL color space demonstrated through extensions to RGB shifts and scale transformations
Honest discussion of limitations including computational expense, parameter-capacity tradeoff, and degenerate lifting cases
weaknesses: Missing formal proof that HSL group convolution (Eq. 16) satisfies equivariance; paper only states 'it can be shown' without justification. Central claim needs rigorous support in main text

Degenerate lifting fundamentally limits information representation when input values equal kc/N, producing at most N/2+1 distinct values (Eq. 19). Impact on real-world performance when datasets contain these values is not characterized

Capacity-equivariance tradeoff inadequately addressed: Figure 8 shows accuracy degradation with increased orders (98.04% → lower), contradicting the benefit of perfect equivariance. While acknowledged, this deserves prominence as fundamental limitation

Limited practical improvements on standard benchmarks: Table 7 shows T³CEN performs worse than LCER on vanilla datasets; advantage exists primarily on synthetic color-shifted test sets. Real-world applicability unclear since most datasets lack artificial color shifts

No computational cost analysis provided despite acknowledging GCNNs are 'typically more computationally expensive'; missing runtime and FLOPs comparisons essential for practical adoption and ICML audience
Design choice of sinusoidal covering map π(θ) = (c/2)sin(θ) lacks justification; why this specific form? Other covering maps unexplored. Sensitivity analysis absent
Degenerate lifting presented as theoretical issue but treated heuristically; entropy-based order selection (H/N) is practical workaround not principled solution
Missing key baseline: no comparison with simple color augmentation during training, which could be simpler and more practical alternative
Dense notation with triple subscripts (gᵢⱼₖ, f₁₁₁) and tilded group actions (Eqs. 12-14) reduces clarity; modified group actions should use clearer notation

Real-world color imbalance (e.g., Camelyon17 non-uniform saturation variation in Figure 15) differs from synthetic uniform shifts; unclear how well method addresses naturally occurring color variations

strengths: Novel application of topological covering maps to achieve perfect equivariance for interval-valued color parameters is mathematically elegant and well-motivated
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across synthetic (3D Shapes, Small NORB) and real-world datasets (CIFAR, Caltech, Camelyon17) with proper reporting of multiple random seeds
Clear visualization and demonstration of equivariance properties (Figures 1-2) effectively show the method's theoretical behavior
Extensive appendix with group theory proofs, implementation details, hyperparameters, and dataset specifications aids reproducibility
Addresses a genuine limitation of prior work (LCER) by observing that intervals lack group structure and proposing a principled solution
weaknesses: Degenerate lifting is a fundamental limitation inadequately addressed: when input = kc/N, only N/2+1 useful representations are produced, contradicting the 'perfect equivariance' claim. This is acknowledged (Eq. 19, Section 5.4) but dismissed with only ~1 paragraph despite being critical
Missing formal proof that the HSL group convolution (Eq. 16) is equivariant—paper states 'It can be shown that...' without demonstration. This is essential to the core claim but left incomplete

Significant performance degradation on vanilla datasets (Table 7): T³CEN-S4L4 achieves 40.87% error on CIFAR-100 vs LCER-H4S3 at 33.27%; on Oxford Pets, 41.30% vs 29.84%. This suggests the equivariance constraints harm real-world performance

Capacity-equivariance tradeoff inadequately analyzed: filter depth is reduced with increasing lifting order, confounding whether improvements come from the covering approach or merely from capacity. Performance degrades with lifting order (Figure 8, best at order 4), but no ablation tests equal-capacity T³CEN

Practical improvements on real-world data are marginal and often within confidence intervals: Camelyon17 saturation shift shows T³CEN-S4 (12.11±2.19%) vs LCER-S3 (16.08±2.68%)—meaningful but not dramatic given vanilla dataset losses
Synthetic dataset results (Table 4, T³CEN-H4S4L4: 0.00% error on HSL-shifted 3D Shapes) raise concerns about realism and potential overfitting to controlled synthetic distributions

Input-dependent coverage via entropy-based metric (Eq. 18) is ad-hoc and lacks rigorous justification. Figure 5 shows coverage varies dramatically across input range, meaning method does not uniformly handle all saturation/luminance values
Incremental contribution over LCER (Yang et al., 2024): same architectural framework, main innovation is the covering map for saturation/luminance. The scope of novelty is relatively narrow

RGB and scale applications (Section 5.4) are underdeveloped with only qualitative results. Authors acknowledge RGB likely has 'poorer performance than HSL' but provide no validation. These feel like afterthoughts

Limited real-world validation: Camelyon17 is the only realistic medical imaging test; no evaluation on naturally color-shifted data or cross-domain scenarios. Most improvements demonstrate only on artificially injected color shifts

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution using topological covering maps to achieve perfect equivariance for interval-valued quantities (saturation/luminance), elegantly solving the approximation problem in prior work
Rigorous mathematical framework with detailed proofs showing hue, saturation, and luminance groups satisfy group axioms
Dramatic improvements in equivariance error (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445 for LCER) demonstrating the approach successfully achieves its theoretical goal

Comprehensive experimental evaluation across synthetic datasets (3D Shapes, MNIST), standard benchmarks (CIFAR, Caltech-101, Oxford Pets, Stanford Cars, STL-10), and medical imaging (Camelyon17, Small NORB) with proper statistical reporting
Insightful analysis of lifting layer coverage with entropy-based approach for principled group order selection
Clear presentation with effective visualizations, particularly Figure 1 (lifting visualization) and Figure 2 (equivariance comparison)
Demonstrates generalizability to RGB channel and scale equivariance, suggesting broader applicability
weaknesses: Computational cost inadequately addressed: no runtime comparisons, memory usage analysis, or training time measurements despite GCNNs being known to be computationally expensive; critical oversight for a practical method

Modest real-world performance improvements: Table 7 shows similar performance on vanilla datasets to LCER/CEConv; Table 5 improvements often <1-2% absolute error (e.g., Caltech-101 saturation: 0.92% improvement), questioning practical value of perfect equivariance

Unresolved capacity-equivariance trade-off: filter depth reduction to maintain parameter count limits gains; Figure 8 shows accuracy drops from 98% to 86% with increasing cardinality, yet paper doesn't investigate constant-capacity comparison where perfect equivariance might show clearer benefits

Degenerate lifting undermines 'perfect equivariance' claim: when input = kc/N, only N/2+1 useful representations available instead of N; non-uniform transformation space coverage; impact on real performance not thoroughly analyzed

Limited novelty over LCER: core HSL-equivariant framework from Yang et al. (2024); main contribution is replacing their translation model with cyclic groups via covering maps—feels somewhat incremental despite mathematical elegance
Missing theoretical justifications: why sine specifically for π(θ)=(c/2)sinθ? Why is entropy metric H/N correct for order selection? Limited discretization sensitivity analysis

Experimental design concerns: different filter counts make it hard to isolate whether improvements come from equivariance approach or architecture; RGB equivariance only qualitative and acknowledged to be worse; scale equivariance preliminary
Claims of improved interpretability lack supporting evidence; no analysis of learned features, latent space properties, or what the network learns differently from LCER
No reproducibility statement about code availability; numerical stability near degenerate points not discussed
Missing failure case analysis: when/why does T³CEN underperform (some Table 7 entries show worse results)? No guidance on when extra complexity is worthwhile

strengths: Novel topological covering approach: Using covering maps to convert interval-valued quantities to cyclic groups is mathematically elegant and represents a genuine advance over prior approximate equivariance methods
Dramatic equivariance improvement: Equivariance error reduced 5+ orders of magnitude (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445) on saturation shifts compared to LCER
Rigorous mathematical framework: Clear presentation of group theory foundations with complete proofs of group axioms for all color channels
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Multiple datasets (synthetic and real), thorough ablations, multiple random seeds, principled order selection via entropy analysis
Honest limitations discussion: Explicitly identifies when method fails (when color is signal) with quantified examples
Generalizability: Approach extends to RGB color space and geometric transformations like scale
weaknesses: Capacity-equivariance trade-off confounds results: Fixed parameter constraint requires reducing filter depth with higher lifting orders, making it difficult to isolate benefits of perfect vs. approximate equivariance from capacity effects; Appendix C.1 shows accuracy drops from 98.04% to 86.06% with increasing order

Modest real-world improvements: On vanilla datasets (Table 9), performance essentially matches LCER; Camelyon17 results are mixed with some configurations underperforming baselines; large gains primarily on synthetic datasets
Significant computational overhead: ~12x slower for full H4S4L4 configuration (1.59 vs 19.38 it/s) and 32GB vs 1GB memory, severely limiting practical applicability

Fundamentally limited applicability: Only effective when color varies between train/test AND varies independently of label; Section 5.5 shows 31.75% error vs 19.13% baseline when color is predictive (tomato ripeness)
Incomplete analysis of redundant representations: Lifting produces redundant outputs at specific values (~0.6-0.9% of pixels); impact on gradient flow and learning dynamics not analyzed
Questionable scale equivariance extension: Equation 24 applies modulo operations to pixel coordinates without properly implementing scale transformations

strengths: Mathematically sound framework using topological covering maps to lift bounded intervals to cyclic groups
Quantitatively lower equivariance error than LCER (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445), with detailed numerical evaluation
Comprehensive experimental evaluation across synthetic and real-world datasets with proper reporting of multiple seeds
Honest and detailed discussion of failure modes and limitations (Section 5.5)
Novel application of covering maps to handle non-cyclic color symmetries in group convolutions
weaknesses: "Perfect equivariance" claim is misleading—the 10⁻⁶ error is floating-point precision, not mathematical perfection; discretization makes it inherently approximate like LCER

Capacity-accuracy confound undermines claims: to maintain fixed parameters, filter depth decreases with lifting order, causing accuracy degradation (Figure 9: error 1.96→9.19 on hue-shift MNIST); confounds equivariance benefits with capacity constraints

Marginal real-world improvements: saturation shift (Table 2) shows near-identical performance (both 0.00 on A/B); Camelyon17 (Table 5) results inconsistent and not clearly superior; vanilla dataset performance often worse than ResNet (Table 9)

Fundamental failure modes: performs 12.6 pp worse than ResNet on tasks where color is predictive (KUTomaData); 4.2 pp worse on same-distribution scenarios (Table 8), revealing when architectural constraint is harmful
Redundant representations occur at 0.57%-0.89% of pixels (Table 10) with unclear impact on learning; lifting layer produces duplicate representations (Eq. 19) unanalyzed
Limited scope: HSL-only; RGB alternative dismissed as having worse performance; scale equivariance shown only qualitatively; most convincing results on synthetic data (3D Shapes), not realistic tasks

Experimental setup questionable: fixed-parameter constraint is unrealistic; artificial color shifts (0.5 reduction in Table 6) don't reflect real distribution changes; practitioners would increase capacity
Incremental contribution: core innovation (replacing clipping with covering maps) is natural extension of Yang et al. (2024); narrow novelty relative to related work in covering spaces

Presentation overstates results: title and abstract emphasize "perfect" equivariance and "better predictive performance" not strongly supported empirically; key limitations (capacity trade-off, failure modes) relegated to later sections

strengths: Novel theoretical contribution: Creative use of topological covering maps to endow interval-valued quantities with cyclic structure, enabling perfect (not approximate) equivariance to saturation and luminance shifts
Dramatic equivariance improvements: 6+ orders of magnitude reduction in equivariance error (4.66×10⁻⁶ vs 0.445) and lifting error (6.33×10⁻⁶ vs 8.65) compared to prior work
Comprehensive experimental evaluation: Diverse datasets, multiple OOD settings, proper statistical reporting with multiple seeds, and rigorous mathematical foundation with formal proofs
Honest limitations discussion: Transparent characterization of failure modes (color-as-signal and no distribution shift) with quantitative analysis, demonstrating methodological maturity
Clear presentation and accessibility: Well-organized writing with effective visualizations (Figures 1-2) and proper mathematical exposition at multiple levels
Principled mathematical treatment: Rigorous group theory foundations with formal proofs of group properties, proper leveraging of established group convolution frameworks
weaknesses: Significant computational overhead inadequately addressed: 32× memory increase (32,842 MiB for H4S4L4) and 12× slowdown in training speed (1.59 it/s vs 19.38 it/s), with filter depth reduced to maintain parameter parity—this confounds architectural benefits with reduced capacity

Confounded experimental design: To keep parameters fixed, filter depth decreases with HSL order, making it impossible to isolate equivariance benefits from capacity penalties. Non-monotonic accuracy in Figure 9 suggests optimization is complex; equal-capacity comparisons needed

Modest practical improvements on real-world tasks: On vanilla datasets (Table 9), T³CEN often underperforms; on color-shifted datasets (Table 6), gains are inconsistent and marginal. Benefits mainly visible in medical imaging, a narrow domain

Unresolved redundant representations: Double-cover creates inherent redundancy at boundary values (Eq. 19), with only N/2+1 useful representations. Impact on learning dynamics unexplored despite 0.6-0.9% of pixels being affected

Group order selection remains heuristic: Entropy-based metric (Figure 6) requires dataset statistics and validation tuning, reducing principled nature. Optimal order is data-dependent with no closed-form solution
Limited justification for design choices: Why sine for π(θ)=(c/2)sin(θ)? Alternatives not discussed. Sensitivity to specific cover selection not analyzed

Incomplete secondary applications: RGB shift equivariance (Section 6) shown only qualitatively; scale equivariance mentioned but not thoroughly evaluated. These feel preliminary rather than integral contributions
Limited reproducibility: No code availability mentioned; lifting layer implementation details for handling redundancy sparse; some architectural modification choices under-documented
